title: Is Summer the New Winter for European Health Systems?
gist: RAND's Robert Romanelli argues European health systems now face a second annual demand peak in summer, not just winter: Europe is warming at twice the global rate (0.53C per decade, 1.59C cumulative over 30 years) and its heat-related mortality has risen nearly 300 percent, from 2.1 to 8.3 per 100,000 between 1990 and 2021. With roughly 90 percent of NHS hospital estates at risk of overheating, June 2026 saw English ward temperatures above 36C, MRI and IT system failures, and the UK Climate Change Committee projects heat-related ED attendances and admissions could triple by 2050 at costs exceeding GBP 4 billion.

insights.claim: Europe is warming at twice the rate of the rest of the planet -- about 0.53C per decade against a global 0.26C between 1994 and 2024 -- leaving the continent roughly 1.59C warmer than 30 years ago versus 0.78C globally.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: The regional warming premium means European adaptation capex requirements are roughly double what global averages imply -- a mispricing risk in infrastructure and insurance models.
insights.locator: The Copernicus Climate Change Service reports

insights.claim: In the span of three days in June 2026 the UK broke three June temperature records, peaking at 37.3C and exceeding the prior record of 35.6C set half a century earlier in 1976, with June records also shattered in France, Spain and Switzerland.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: A 1.7C break of a 50-year-old record across multiple countries simultaneously suggests distribution shift rather than tail noise -- adaptation demand arrives sooner than gradualist models assume.
insights.locator: In the span of three days, the UK broke three temperature records

insights.claim: Heatwaves are becoming not only more frequent but more severe, longer lasting and wider in geographic coverage, and rapid-onset heat spikes are becoming more common -- some UK locations saw temperature increases of 10C in just two days during the June heatwave.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: Rate-of-change, not just peak level, breaks systems designed for gradual transitions -- it stresses grid, cooling and staffing response times specifically.

insights.claim: Global heat-related mortality rose from 4.9 to 7.1 per 100,000 persons between 1990 and 2021, a 45 percent increase, according to the 2025 Lancet Countdown Report.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: A hard baseline for actuarial and health-system modelling of climate mortality trends.
insights.locator: According to the 2025 Lancet Countdown Report

insights.claim: European heat-related mortality rose from 2.1 to 8.3 per 100,000 persons between 1990 and 2021, a rise of nearly 300 percent -- Europe went from below the global rate to above it over the period.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: The crossover is the key signal: Europe's built environment and demographics amplify heat mortality, making it the highest-beta region for heat-health policy and spending.
insights.locator: Again, Europe is taking the brunt

insights.claim: Of the roughly half a million heat-related deaths per year globally between 2000 and 2019, 36 percent occurred in Europe, despite the continent comprising only about 9 percent of the global population.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: A fourfold over-representation quantifies Europe's structural vulnerability -- likely driven by age profile and absence of cooling infrastructure, both investable gaps.

themes.theme: Summer as a second demand peak

insights.claim: Scenes normally associated with December or January in European hospitals -- queuing ambulances, patients on trolleys in corridors, cancelled elective procedures and overwhelmed staff -- are now becoming common in summer months during heatwaves.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: A second annual demand peak destroys the winter-crisis planning model; capacity, agency staffing and elective-backlog economics all need reforecasting.

insights.claim: Hot weather drives health demand through heat stress and exacerbations of chronic conditions including cardiovascular disease, diabetes, kidney disease, asthma and frailty -- a different clinical mix from winter's acute respiratory illness and icy-weather injuries.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: Different clinical mix means different drug, device and staffing demand in summer surges -- not simply more of the winter pattern.

insights.claim: An Oxford University study using more than 4 million patient records from English general practices between 2007 and 2019 found that very hot days -- defined as above 23C -- are associated with spikes in same-day health service utilisation and mortality.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: The 23C threshold is remarkably low and same-day, meaning surge events are far more frequent than headline heatwave counts suggest.
insights.locator: A recent study published by Oxford University

insights.claim: A Portuguese study of 12 million hospital records between 2000 and 2018 found hospital admissions increased nearly 20 percent on heatwave days, with children disproportionately affected.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: A ~20 percent admissions spike is a usable elasticity for forecasting bed-day demand and capacity costs across southern Europe.
insights.locator: Another study from Portugal examining 12 million hospital records

insights.claim: The UK Climate Change Committee's fourth independent assessment of UK climate risk reports that heat-related emergency department attendances and hospital admissions could triple by 2050, with costs potentially exceeding GBP 4 billion.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: An official, quantified fiscal liability that will feature in NHS spending settlements -- a forward indicator for health estates and cooling procurement.
insights.locator: The Climate Change Committee, in their recently released fourth independent assessment

insights.claim: An estimated 90 percent of NHS hospital estates -- largely older buildings lacking centralised air-cooling systems -- are at risk of overheating and vulnerable to heatwaves, a condition shared by many European hospitals including in wealthy countries like Germany.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: A near-universal retrofit gap across European health estates -- one of the clearest identified adaptation capex pipelines in public infrastructure.
insights.locator: In the UK, an estimated 90 percent of NHS hospital estates

insights.claim: Even where hospitals do have centralised air-cooling, those systems cannot cope under extreme temperatures, meaning existing cooling installations do not eliminate heat risk.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: Design-standard obsolescence, not just absence of equipment -- implying replacement and upsizing demand rather than only first-time installation.
insights.locator: But even in countries where hospitals have centralized air-cooling

insights.claim: During the June 2026 heatwave, hospital ward temperatures rose upward of 36C in parts of England, with staff struggling to keep patients hydrated and stabilised.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: Ward temperature is becoming a patient-safety and regulatory metric in its own right -- expect standards and enforcement to follow.
insights.locator: As hospital ward temperatures rose upward of 36°C

insights.claim: Medical imaging devices such as MRIs and IT systems also failed to work during the heatwave, slowing patient flow and producing longer waits and cancelled appointments and treatments.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: Heat is now an equipment-uptime risk, not only a clinical one -- service contracts, imaging utilisation rates and diagnostic throughput are all exposed.
insights.locator: Medical imagining devices, like MRIs, and IT systems also failed

insights.claim: During a heatwave in June 2022, London hospitals suffered an IT outage caused by cooling system failures at two of their data centres, leading to treatment delays and GBP 1.5 million in additional costs to the English NHS.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: A costed precedent linking datacentre cooling failure to clinical disruption -- directly relevant to healthcare IT resilience spend and to datacentre cooling suppliers generally.

insights.claim: The World Health Organization released a second edition of Heat-Health Action Plans last month as a guidance document and implementation framework for treating extreme heat as a public health threat, emphasising building resilience into health systems.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: An international framework typically precedes national procurement programmes -- the template governments will cite when funding heat resilience.

insights.claim: Building climate resilience into European health systems requires both absorbing increased service demand and keeping hospitals physically safe environments, and will likely require substantial long-term investment -- with the cost of doing nothing far greater.
insights.speaker: Robert J. Romanelli
insights.so_what: Frames heat adaptation as a multi-year public capex commitment rather than emergency response -- the structural case for cooling, estates and resilience contractors.
insights.quote: Will European governments move at pace to protect its fragile health system infrastructure against climate change?
insights.locator: To remain resilient to the impacts of climate change
